title: Drama therapy to promote well-being and resilience in oncological care and aftercare with breast cancer patients.
summary:
With around 70,000 new cases every year, breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosis among women in Germany; Men are also affected, although with lower prevalence. For many of those affected, the diagnosis represents a profound life crisis, which is accompanied by fears, loss of control and changed body perception. The DSM-5 and ICD-10 often classify the psychological reactions to cancer as acute stress or stress disorder. For the early detection of psychosocial stress, the distress value is used in a clinical context as a standardized procedure to determine the need for support. Psycho-oncological interventions are now an integral part of oncological care, and artistic therapies are increasingly being integrated into follow-up treatment. Despite the positive findings on the effectiveness of artistic therapies, there is a lack of research regarding the specific mechanisms and effects of theater therapy in oncological aftercare. This work therefore examines the potential impact factors and resilience-promoting effects of theater therapy in breast cancer patients.
Drama therapy is an action- and body-oriented process that goes beyond verbal expression and offers a protected framework for emotional processing through aesthetic distance. It is part of the artistic therapies that are recognized in the S3 guidelines for early detection, diagnosis, therapy and aftercare of breast cancer as a supportive measure to improve quality of life and psychosocial stabilization. However, there is currently no specific recommendation for drama therapy because the research on drama-based forms of therapy is limited. International studies demonstrate the effectiveness of drama therapy interventions in various age groups and contexts to reduce psychological stress. A WHO study also points to the positive effects of artistic therapies on mental health.  Drama therapy is based on the assumption that creative and scenic forms of expression can initiate processes of change. Jones (1996) identified nine fundamental change processes that are common to all drama therapy approaches. These were found in a Delphi study by Frydman et al. (2022) revised so that seven core processes of drama therapy emerged: active witnessing, distancing, dramatic play, dramatic projection, embodiment, engagement in dramatic reality and multidimensional relationship.
Particularly in drama therapy, narratives are created, questioned and transformed, creating new roles and meanings. In psycho-oncological support, narrative work can enable patients to reconstruct their illness history and develop new perspectives. Research at the interface between medicine and creative therapies is also examined. Creative therapies are becoming increasingly important in psycho-oncological care. Studies show that they can reduce emotional distress, promote resilience and improve patients' quality of life. Building on these findings, the specific potential of drama therapy for breast cancer patients will be researched.

interventions.name: The main aim of this study is to analyze the drama therapy intervention in the oncological care and follow-up care of breast cancer patients with regard to its mechanisms of action and effects. Employees who work in the healthcare sector serve as the control group/ observation group. Men are also included.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Breast cancer patients aged 18 to 75 who are in the care or follow-up care. Written consent to participate in the study must also have been given.
Exclusion criteria:
Participants who are excluded due to serious mental illnesses (such as schizophrenia or acute psychoses) or cognitive limitations that would make active participation in theater therapy difficult do not meet the inclusion criteria. Men with breast cancer are also excluded in order to examine a homogeneous group that can deal with the female aspect and consequences of the disease.
